explanation:
## Forwards

```cpp
int firstIndexOf(const std::vector<int>& v, int target)
{
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i)
        if (v[i] == target) return static_cast<int>(i);
    return -1;
}
```

Nothing surprising: compare each element, return the index of the first match,
return -1 if the loop finishes. The `static_cast<int>` is there because `i` is
`std::size_t` and the return type is `int` - narrowing without a cast is what
`-Wconversion` complains about, and writing the cast is a way of saying "yes, I
know `n` is small enough".

## Backwards, and the loop that never ends

The natural translation of "start at the last index and count down" is a bug:

```cpp
for (std::size_t i = v.size() - 1; i >= 0; --i)     // broken twice over
    if (v[i] == target) return static_cast<int>(i);
```

Two separate failures, both caused by `std::size_t` being **unsigned**:

**`i >= 0` is always true.** An unsigned value cannot be negative, so the loop
condition can never become false. GCC says so with `-Wtype-limits`, part of
`-Wextra`: *comparison of unsigned expression in '>= 0' is always true*.

**`--i` at `i == 0` wraps.** Unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap modulo 2^64,
so `0 - 1` is 18446744073709551615. The loop then evaluates
`v[18446744073709551615]`, which is an address roughly 147 exabytes past the
array. In practice the program segfaults - but only *in practice*: reading out of
bounds is undefined behaviour, so a smaller overrun may read whatever happens to
be in memory and keep going with plausible garbage.

**And on an empty vector it is worse.** `v.size() - 1` is already the huge value
before the loop body ever runs, so the very first `v[i]` is out of bounds.

## Two safe ways to write it

**A one-past-the-end counter**, which is what the reference does:

```cpp
for (std::size_t i = v.size(); i > 0; --i)
    if (v[i - 1] == target) return static_cast<int>(i - 1);
```

`i` runs from `size()` down to 1, so it never reaches 0 and never wraps. The
element is `v[i - 1]`, and the subtraction is safe because the condition
guarantees `i >= 1`. On an empty vector `i` starts at 0, `i > 0` is false, and
the loop body never runs.

**A signed index**, which is fine when the size fits:

```cpp
for (int i = static_cast<int>(v.size()) - 1; i >= 0; --i)
    if (v[i] == target) return i;
```

Now `i >= 0` means what it looks like, because `int` can be negative. This reads
more naturally and is perfectly correct for `n` up to two billion. It is why
some large codebases - Google's among them - prefer signed integers for indices
and sizes, and why `std::ssize` was added in C++20 to get a signed size without
a cast.

The lesson generalises past this loop: **an unsigned type does not mean "a number
that cannot be negative", it means "a number that silently becomes enormous
instead".** Any subtraction on an unsigned value is a place to stop and check.

## Two loops or one

Both answers could come from a single pass:

```cpp
int f{ -1 }, l{ -1 };
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i)
    if (v[i] == target) { if (f < 0) f = static_cast<int>(i); l = static_cast<int>(i); }
```

One traversal instead of two, and for a vector in cache that is roughly twice as
fast. It also loses the early exit: `firstIndexOf` on a match at index 0 stops
immediately, where the combined loop always walks the whole array.

Two named functions were chosen here because each one is independently testable
and the backward loop is the thing being practised. Either is defensible; the
single pass is what you would write if this were on a hot path.

## -1 as "not found", and why it is a weak habit

It works here because an *index* is never negative, so -1 cannot be mistaken for
a real answer. That is the condition the convention depends on, and it is easy to
outgrow: the moment the function returns a *value* from the array rather than an
index, -1 becomes a legitimate element and the sentinel becomes a bug. The hidden
case with `-1` in the data is a reminder of how close that is.

The modern alternatives say "or nothing" in the type:

```cpp
std::optional<std::size_t> firstIndexOf(...);   // has_value() or not
```

and the standard library's own answer is a past-the-end iterator:

```cpp
auto it = std::find(v.begin(), v.end(), target);
if (it == v.end()) { /* absent */ }
else               { std::size_t idx = static_cast<std::size_t>(it - v.begin()); }
```

`v.end()` is a position that exists and cannot be dereferenced, so "not found" is
represented without stealing a value from the result space. That is the same
half-open-range idea as the loop above, used for a different purpose.

## Python, for comparison

```python
for i in range(len(v) - 1, -1, -1):
    if v[i] == target:
        return i
```

This is safe, because Python integers are arbitrary-precision and signed -
`len(v) - 1` on an empty list is `-1`, and `range(-1, -1, -1)` is simply empty.
The entire class of bug above does not exist. That is worth seeing side by side:
the C++ version is not harder because C++ is clumsy, it is harder because the
index is a fixed-width machine integer, which is also why the C++ version
compiles to a single pointer decrement.
